changed.previousSay: Budget acceptance still would not establish a safe prompt. Mean development gains cannot compensate for a separately declared forbidden-serve limit. Divide observed forbidden serves by the relevant cases and compare that rate with its cap. Keep the action-and-record metric, family split, intermediate-trace checks and fresh final evaluation. Bind the approved prompt to its actual runtime model and host authorization. You can now inspect what prompt search changes, count the requests it needs and distinguish a compiled artifact from an earned release.

A deployment assistant reads an approval record for rolling back payment-tests. An engineer asks whether that same record also permits deploying payment-service. A loose evaluator spots the approval and gives the answer credit.

That score can steer prompt search toward a confident mistake. We will separate the program's inputs and outputs, the behavior its metric rewards, and the data used to choose a candidate. Then we will open the held-out result only after the choice is frozen.
For the rollback request, the correct pair is serve with its approval record. For deployment, the supported pair is abstain with no record attached.
The metric awards a point only when both fields match. The unsupported deployment scores zero even though the answer names a real policy record. Search is only as useful as this target.

Training examples can seed demonstrations and show the program's task. A development set guides candidate search and comparisons. Keep the private test out of those choices until the prompt is frozen.

Group paraphrases of the same policy family together when the goal is transfer to unseen policies. Otherwise near-identical cases can cross the boundary and make the final score look more transferable than it is. A declared-family metadata check cannot discover semantic duplicates assigned different family IDs.

A bootstrap optimizer can run a teacher program on training cases and keep predictor traces whose metric passes its acceptance rule. The accepted trace can become a few-shot demonstration in the compiled program.

This fixture uses a binary metric, so the trace must score one. A truthy partial score can admit a weak example in some optimizer configurations. Inspect the threshold and the recorded intermediate steps before the examples teach the next prompt.

One authored case asks about deploying payment-service. Candidate A sees approval-4412 and predicts SERVE, though the record covers a test rollback. The exact action-and-record metric scores zero. We revise the instruction to check action and target, then rerun the case. Candidate B abstains with no record and earns one point.

Separately, an authored twenty-case teaching fixture gives baseline fourteen of twenty and compiled-a nineteen of twenty. Those aggregate totals select compiled-a while weights stay fixed. A real run needs its own model calls, cache policy, sampling settings, and scorer version.
On development, the baseline gets fourteen of twenty cases right and compiled-a gets nineteen. Search selects compiled-a before the private test lane opens.

On the held-out fixture, the ordering reverses: baseline leads while compiled-a falls behind. A small validation set can reward a narrow phrasing pattern, so keep the final test fresh after prompt changes.
A reversal deserves case-level inspection and uncertainty estimates. Counts alone cannot tell whether the cause is selection noise, a distribution shift, or a defect in the metric.
After selection, save the compiled program with its instructions and demonstrations. Record the dataset, metric, optimizer, model, and settings so another run can reconstruct the comparison.

When loading the artifact, inspect the predictor's attached language model. Bind the intended runtime model explicitly, then test the loaded program with the same output contract and a fresh policy case.

Bootstrap Few Shot collects accepted predictor traces up to its limits and can stop before visiting every case. In a multi-stage program, a correct final answer may admit intermediate recorded steps too. Review those steps for support and causal relevance. In pinned version three point four point zero, an absent or zero metric threshold takes the score’s truthiness. A partial score of zero point five, a negative number and NaN are truthy. With no metric configured, successful teacher executions are accepted without a quality check. A meaningful nonzero threshold helps only when the metric catches the important error.

Bootstrap Random Search evaluates alternative demonstration subsets. COPRO searches predictor instructions and output prefixes using candidate scores and search history; its trainset argument is development evaluation data, not an automatic final holdout. MIPRO Version Two jointly searches instructions and demonstrations across predictors, using data-grounded proposals and a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator search through Optuna. These prompt optimizers keep model weights fixed.

GEPA reflects on recorded execution feedback to propose revised predictor instructions. Its pinned metric contract needs five arguments: gold, prediction, trace, predictor name and predictor trace. It may return a scalar or a score with useful textual feedback. Our three-argument metric therefore needs an adapter. An optional program-trace argument supports Flex submodules, while the five-argument contract remains. Reflection proposes text; it does not directly certify or repair the model’s internal reasoning.

Budget the complete search. Forty full candidate evaluations across fifty validation cases give two thousand logical program executions. Pinned MIPRO also evaluates the default program first, adding fifty. The total is two thousand fifty before teacher bootstrapping or instruction proposals. Minibatching and periodic full evaluations change that accounting. This is a count calculation, not an executed model search.

A logical program execution can contain several predictors and a model-backed judge. In a separate no-cache, no-retry toy, two predictors plus one judge per execution turn two thousand fifty executions into six thousand one hundred fifty requests, before teacher and proposer work. Actual cache hits can remove requests, retries can add them and different roles can use different prices. Record role, input and output usage and the request’s observed outcome.

Enforce hard spend and latency caps outside the optimizer. Unknown remote outcomes may still consume budget and need reconciliation. Adding two thousand five hundred logical input tokens at one hundred requests per second gives two hundred fifty thousand extra logical input tokens per second. This does not determine uncached billable tokens, dollars or first-token latency. Measure quality, serving behavior and dated cost estimates for the actual artifact and model.

State-only JSON stores compiled instructions, demonstrations, signature metadata and model settings. Restore it into the matching reviewed Python program. The actual serialization fixture restores two demonstrations and its attached model A. A global context containing model B leaves model A attached. Explicitly call set L M with the intended runtime model, then evaluate that changed artifact-model pair.

The pinned serializer omits the top-level API key but preserves the fixture’s nested Authorization header string. Demonstrations, instructions, arbitrary configuration and custom model state can also hold sensitive data. Inspect the complete artifact before sharing it. These are placeholder strings in a local test, not real credentials or evidence that arbitrary secrets are removed.

Whole-program persistence uses cloudpickle and loading an untrusted pickle can execute code. State-only JSON avoids that deserialization mechanism but still depends on compatible reviewed code, dependencies and approved configuration. Retain code and artifact digests, the effective model and engine, data/scorer versions, evaluation evidence and a checked rollback target. A digest identifies bytes; it does not authenticate approval or enforce retention.

Test a new fictional plan. It evaluates eight full trials over twenty-four cases and includes one baseline. How many logical program executions are planned? Pause. There are nine times twenty-four, or two hundred sixteen. Assume every execution makes two predictor calls and one judge call, with no cache hits or retries. Teacher work adds twelve requests and proposal work adds nine. Predict the complete request count and compare it with a host cap of six hundred fifty.

Two hundred sixteen times three gives six hundred forty-eight, plus twelve and nine gives six hundred sixty-nine. The plan exceeds the six hundred fifty request cap by nineteen before it starts. Refuse the unbudgeted plan or deliberately reduce its search and evaluate that revised protocol. The numbers are an authored count example, rather than a provider invoice or measured search result.

Next, model versioning binds that compiled artifact to its model, policy, retrieval data and runtime, then verifies which complete release actually serves each request.

The approval on the desk permits a rollback of payment-tests. Now read the engineer’s request on the line below. Deploy payment-service. The assistant answers serve and quotes the approval number. A grader finds that number and gives the answer credit. Would you serve this request or abstain?

It should abstain. Read down the action column, then the target column. Both changed. The grader gave the assistant a point for quoting a record that rules out this deployment. Search could reward an instruction that repeats the ID on every request. Let's change what earns a point.

Return to the deployment request. The baseline instruction says to find an approval and give its ID. It serves with the rollback record. The exact action-and-record metric scores zero. Change just the instruction. Tell the predictor to match both action and target and to abstain if either lacks support. With the same inputs, which route and record should it return? Read down the two columns. Candidate B abstains with no record and earns one point.

This was a worked replay. A real prompt change may produce a different reply. Take a separate set of illustrative counts. Here are the development scores, baseline fourteen of twenty and compiled-a nineteen of twenty. Which prompt would you freeze? Compare the two rows. Those aggregate totals select compiled-a while weights stay fixed. How will it do on fresh cases?
Freeze Compiled A. It won on development. The two programs now face twenty held-out cases that played no part in that choice. Keep the selected prompt marked while we open the results.

On the new cases the baseline gets sixteen right. On the held-out fixture, the ordering reverses: baseline leads while compiled-a falls behind. Compiled A got thirteen right. Its five-case lead on development has become a three-case deficit on test. These are supplied counts. They tell us which program scored higher on each sample.

beats.say: Watch the first digit as this ZIP code comes off the envelope. Prompt A returns a number and drops the zero. Prompt B copies all five digits. The grader compares each answer with the ZIP code as a number. Which prompt gets a point?

Both get a point. As numbers, the two answers are equal. Switch the grader to an exact text match. Now only prompt B earns the point. The outputs stayed the same. Changing what earned a point changed which prompt won.

Score the rollback first. Its label calls for serve and record forty-four twelve. The assistant gets the route right but cites record ninety-nine ninety-nine. Our grader compares the two fields to the reviewed label. How many points should this reply get?

Zero points. The route agrees, but the records differ. Put the approved ID back. The metric awards a point only when both fields match. Keep that last reply. Change the question to deployment. The reviewed answer changes to abstain with an empty ID. The unsupported deployment scores zero.
The assistant cited the same real approval both times. It only supports the rollback. If a task allows several valid records, give the grader that approved set. A good grader needs good labels.

Use training cases to build examples. Use development cases to choose among prompts. Save the test for the frozen choice. Here two training requests ask about the same approval in different words. They belong to one policy family.

Look at the new request in the test column. Its request number is different. Its approval number already appears in training. How can we keep this test fresh? Group paraphrases of the same policy family together. A checker catches matching family IDs. If someone gave two paraphrases different family IDs, the metadata check could pass. Inspect the underlying policies too.

Try another way to fill the example slots. Let a teacher answer the training questions and record its steps. On the rollback, it answers serve with the approved record. Both fields match. At a threshold of one, this trace passes. The accepted trace can become a few-shot demonstration in the compiled program. Look at the copied predictor step. It still names the rollback and its approval.
Now ask the teacher about deploying payment-service. It gives the same reply. The reviewed label is abstain with an empty ID. Does the rollback example stay in the prompt?

It stays. The deployment scores zero, so its trace is discarded. Two teacher replies left one bootstrapped example. The original student still has zero. Now imagine a two-step teacher whose final answer is right by chance. Check each recorded step before you teach another predictor to repeat it.

Return to the deployment request. The baseline instruction says to find an approval and give its ID. It serves with the rollback record. The exact action-and-record metric scores zero. Change just the instruction. Tell the predictor to match both action and target and to abstain if either lacks support. With the same inputs, which route and record should it return?
Candidate B abstains with no record and earns one point.
Now compare two prompts across twenty development cases. Both use the same model weights. The baseline gets fourteen right. Compiled A gets nineteen. Which prompt would you freeze for the test?
Freeze Compiled A. It got five more cases right.
Keep that choice fixed. Both prompts now face twenty cases the search never saw. Does Compiled A keep its lead?
The baseline gets sixteen right. Compiled A gets thirteen. Its five-case lead on development has become a three-case deficit on test.

To investigate, line up both answers for each request. Check the labels, compare policy families, and estimate uncertainty on the paired results. A small sample or a different mix of policies could change the order. If you edit the prompt after seeing these cases, save a fresh test for the next frozen prompt.
Return to the copy with two labeled examples. Save its prompt with model A attached. Load it into the same program class. Now set the global default to model B. Which model would this predictor call?

Model A. The predictor already has its own attachment. Bind the intended runtime model explicitly. Here that's model B. Now the predictor reports B. Keep the prompt fixed and evaluate that exact combination before serving it.

Look inside a two-step teacher. Its first step says the approval covers deployment. Its final reply happens to abstain with an empty ID. A grader that checks just the final pair gives it one. The unsupported first step can now enter a demonstration too. Review it against the policy. Collection can stop when the example slots fill, even if training cases remain. What if the grader returns a fraction? In this version, a zero or missing threshold tests the score’s truth value. A partial score of zero point five, a negative number and NaN are truthy.

Now try a separate probe. Give both traces half a point, including the bad deployment. With a zero threshold, half a point lets both traces through. Set the threshold to one and neither gets in. With no metric at all, a successful execution passes unchecked. Choose a threshold and a metric that actually catches the error.

You can search different parts of this program with the same model weights. Bootstrap Random Search tries different subsets of examples. COPRO searches instructions and output prefixes using scores from earlier trials. Its trainset argument supplies development cases. MIPRO version two searches instructions and examples together across predictors. It proposes instructions from the data and uses Optuna’s Tree-structured Parzen Estimator to choose combinations to try.

GEPA can use a written critique of a recorded run. To point to the bad step, its metric takes five arguments, the label, prediction, trace, predictor name and predictor trace. Adapt our three-argument metric to that interface. It can return a scalar, or a score and feedback like “check which target the approval names.” The optional program trace serves Flex submodules. The critique proposes a new instruction that still needs evaluation.

Take a larger plan with forty full trials and fifty validation cases. That’s two thousand logical program executions for the candidates. MIPRO also scores the default program first, adding fifty. That brings us to two thousand fifty executions. Minibatches and periodic full evaluations would change this count.

What does one execution cost? Suppose it makes two predictor requests and one judge request. With one answer per call, no cache hits and no retries, those three calls turn two thousand fifty executions into six thousand one hundred fifty requests. Teacher and proposal calls are extra. Keep the executions fixed. One cache hit saves one request. If instead one call takes an extra attempt, add one request to the original total.

The host enforces spend and latency caps. A timed-out request may still incur a charge. Reconcile its outcome. Suppose longer demonstrations add tokens to every request. Adding two thousand five hundred logical input tokens at one hundred requests per second gives two hundred fifty thousand extra logical input tokens per second. To price it, measure actual input and output usage by role, including cached input, and use the applicable rates. Measure first-token latency on the serving system.

Look inside that same JSON file. It stores the instruction, demonstrations, signature metadata and model settings. The actual serialization fixture restores two demonstrations and its attached model A. Both examples travel with the file. Set the global default to B and the attachment stays A. Explicitly call set L M with the intended runtime model. Now the loaded copy uses B. What else made it into the file?

The pinned serializer omits the top-level API key. Open the nested configuration. The same serializer preserves the fixture’s nested Authorization header string. Read the demonstrations and instructions too. They can contain sensitive text. Inspect and sanitize the whole saved state before sharing it, then evaluate the approved copy.

Whole-program files use cloudpickle. An untrusted pickle can execute code when loaded. State-only JSON needs compatible reviewed code, dependencies and configuration. Keep the code and artifact digests with the effective model and engine, data and scorer versions, evaluation evidence and a checked rollback target. A digest identifies the bytes. Record approval separately and retain the approved files.

Here’s a smaller plan. Run eight full trials and one baseline over twenty-four cases each. Every execution makes two predictor calls and one judge call. Assume one answer per call, no cache hits and no retries. Allow twelve teacher requests and nine proposal requests for the whole search. The host allows six hundred fifty requests. Would you start?

Nine runs through twenty-four cases make two hundred sixteen executions. Three calls each give six hundred forty-eight requests. Add the teacher and proposer and the total reaches six hundred sixty-nine. The plan exceeds the six hundred fifty request cap by nineteen before it starts.

Try seven trials instead. Keep the baseline and the same overhead. One fewer pass saves seventy-two requests. The revised plan needs five hundred ninety-seven. It fits. That buys a smaller search. You still have to establish which prompt it chose and how that prompt behaves.
